This is the **living page** of the book. Chapters 1 to 4 describe how the system
works and why; this page records what *changed*, newest first, with the lesson
attached.

It is the mechanism that keeps the book honest. A decision chapter that is never
updated is a museum; this page is the changelog that forces the rest of the book
to be revisited whenever something moves.

**Last entry:** 2026-10-04 · **Entries:** 5 · **Newest first**

## How to add an entry {#sec-log-howto}

Append to the **top** of the list, directly under this line:

1. Pick a date (the day of the change, not the day you are writing it up).
2. Copy the template below verbatim and fill it in.
3. Make the *lesson* sentence the point. If the entry cannot state a rule or a
   correction, it is a changelog line, not a log entry.
4. If the change invalidates something in a chapter, fix the chapter in the same
   commit. A log entry that leaves the book contradicting itself is worse than no
   entry.
5. Re-render and re-run the smoke test (see `doc/README.md`).

### Entry template {#sec-log-template}

Copy everything between the rules below into a new `## YYYY-MM-DD — <title>`
section.

````markdown
## YYYY-MM-DD — <short title>

**What changed.** One or two sentences. Name the subsystem and the observable
behaviour change. Reference the commit by short hash if there is one.

**Why.** The situation that made the change necessary — a limit reached, a bug
seen, a capability needed.

**Lesson / correction.** The rule that comes out of it, phrased as an instruction
to the next person (or the next run). This is the part future readers care
about.

**Where it lives.** The files that were touched, relative to the repository root.
````

### House rules for entries {#sec-log-rules}

- **Evidence, not narrative.** Point at code, a commit, or an observable
  behaviour. If neither exists, the entry is not ready.
- **No personal information.** The same rules as the rest of the book: no names,
  no identifiers, no credentials, no private paths. See `doc/README.md`.
- **Corrections are welcome, mistakes are not hidden.** An entry that records
  "this was wrong, here is the rule now" is more valuable than one that never
  records a mistake.
- **One entry per decision, not per commit.** A commit that touches three files for
  one reason is one entry.

## 2026-10-04 — Session topics and the backend channel (0.15.0) {#log-0150}

**What changed.** Two features in one release. First, a session *topic* is now
carried on the reply itself: the prompt instructs the model to end every final
user-facing response with exactly one trailing machine line naming a topic (or
explicitly clearing it), and the gateway strips that line, applies it to session
metadata, and persists it. Second, the backend channel landed — a loopback-only,
token-gated event endpoint plus a read-only tailer over the jobs database, both
waking isolated per-job sessions. A lightweight SQLite sessions index landed with
it so listing sessions stops reading every transcript. Reference: `553c00e`.

**Why.** Sessions had no subject line, so a long-lived conversation was
unidentifiable in the dashboard and in any listing. And the assistant could only be
started by a person in a chat, or on a schedule — automated work had no way to
wake it.

**Lesson / correction.** Machine-readable lines must be stripped at the edge,
before anything else touches the content, and they must never be visible in user
facing text. When the model fails to emit one, the gateway treats it as a no-op
rather than an error: a missing signal degrades, it does not fail. And a
user-locked value must never be overwritten by a model-suggested one — that
asymmetry has to be encoded, not assumed.

**Where it lives.** `sarathy/agent/loop.py`, `sarathy/agent/context.py`,
`sarathy/agent/builtin_commands.py`, `sarathy/channels/backend.py`,
`sarathy/channels/manager.py`, `sarathy/config/schema.py`,
`sarathy/session/manager.py`.

## 2026-09-23 — Dashboard "new chat" parity, in four commits {#log-parity}

**What changed.** The dashboard's new-chat action was brought to parity with the
chat command, in sequence: archive the session the way the chat side does
(`0138361`), persist the rotation and fix mobile layout and cache headers
(`cade0bc`), archive the *live cached* session rather than the stale on-disk copy
(`9d9747c`), and confirm it to the user with a success toast (`9d535f2`).

**Why.** The mechanism existed and was wrong. Because the live conversation lives
in memory and is only flushed to disk opportunistically, the rotation archived an
old snapshot — every message since the last save was silently dropped from the
archive — and never persisted the fresh session, so a reload resurrected the
conversation that was supposed to be gone. Two archive files of identical size
were the symptom that gave it away.

**Lesson / correction.** *A rotation must archive what is actually in memory, not
what happens to be on disk.* When a component caches, the cache is the truth and
the file is a lagging copy — code that reads the file to make a destructive
decision is operating on stale data. And parity is behaviour **plus**
confirmation: a feature that works but does not say it happened is not finished.
Walk both products end to end; do not compare mechanisms.

**Where it lives.** `sarathy/session/manager.py`, the dashboard session view and
its API handlers.

## 2026-09-22 — Per-session concurrency replaces the global dispatch lock {#log-concurrency}

**What changed.** A single dispatch lock was replaced with three layers: a global
lock for runtime hot-reload and configuration mutation, a semaphore capping
concurrent sessions, and a per-session lock registry that creates locks on demand
and drops them when idle. Matching guards were added around memory writes, the
scheduler's job list, and the subagent task registry. Reference: `5929cc3`.

**Why.** One slow turn blocked every other conversation — including side
questions and background work. The assistant was effectively single-lane.

**Lesson / correction.** Removing a global lock does not remove the need for
locking; it moves the lock onto the objects that are genuinely shared. Lock
*ordering* has to be written down at the point of acquisition, and the tests have
to cover it: parallelism across sessions, ordering within a session, registry
cleanup, cancellation isolation, and the global cap. A lock registry that never
shrinks is a slow leak.

**Where it lives.** `sarathy/agent/loop.py`, `sarathy/session/memory.py`,
`sarathy/cron/service.py`, `sarathy/agent/subagent.py`, `tests/test_session_concurrency.py`.

---

## 2026-09-22 — Session epochs make "new conversation" reset the cost ledger {#log-epoch}

**What changed.** Usage accounting gained an epoch: every usage row records the
epoch that was current at the time, a small table holds the authoritative current
epoch per session, and starting a new conversation advances it. The compact usage
footer now reports the cost of the current conversation rather than of all
time. References: `33f455b`, `3c107b1`, `054a211`.

**Why.** Cost was attributed to the session key, which lives for the whole life of
a chat. Starting a new conversation did not and could not reset the number without
deleting history.

**Lesson / correction.** *Attribute to the conversation, key on the identity.*
Adding a dimension beat mutating history: the ledger stays append-only, and the
authoritative epoch lives outside it so a crash between "advance" and "next turn"
cannot desynchronise. Schema changes ship as numbered, idempotent migrations that
re-check for existing columns.

**Where it lives.** `sarathy/usage/store.py`, `sarathy/usage/footer.py`,
`sarathy/agent/loop.py`.

---

## 2026-09-20 — Cron sessions rotate at the trim cap, and archives get retention {#log-cron-cap}

**What changed.** Scheduled jobs now rotate their session *between* runs rather
than never; the check runs on both the cached and the cold-load path; cron
sessions are exempt from the save-time trim so their full history reaches the
archive; and `prune_archives()` added an explicit retention policy that keeps
anything still unverified. Reference: `67a3176`.

**Why.** A cron session reuses one stable key and was being trimmed to the cap on
every save, so the length could never reach the rotation threshold. The session
was reused forever on a rolling window of stale context until a run's prompt
overflowed — and the run reported success while producing nothing.

**Lesson / correction.** *A cap and a rotation threshold are different numbers; if
the cap keeps the value below the threshold, the rotation is dead code.* Verify
that a limit can actually be reached before relying on the behaviour behind it.
Rotation points must also respect the unit of work — a cron session may rotate
between runs, never mid-run, because a mid-run rotation destroys the run's own
context. And any directory that grows without a reaper needs an explicit retention
policy.

**Where it lives.** `sarathy/session/manager.py`, `tests/test_session_rotation.py`.

## Seeded from the history {#log-seed}

These five entries were written from the commit history on 2026-10-04, working
backwards from the release that prompted this book. They are deliberately short
and deliberately specific: the point of an entry is the *lesson*, and a lesson
that needs three paragraphs is usually a chapter section instead. Later entries
should be written at the moment the decision is made, while the reasoning is still
fresh — that is the only time the "why" is fully available.
